introduction-the-distributed-nightmare.core: In distributed systems you can't upgrade everything at once: services, clients and databases change at different times. Releases must be sequenced so every intermediate state stays compatible.

first_principles.problem: A big-bang release that changes the API, the database and three services together fails partway, leaving an incompatible mix.
truths: Old and new versions coexist during rollout.
Data changes are the hardest to reverse.

analogy.title: Moving house room by room
analogy.story: Instead of moving everything in one day, you set up the new place gradually while the old one still works.
analogy.breaks: Incremental changes take more steps and more calendar time.

example.title: Renaming a column
flow: Big bang: rename + deploy → old pods crash
Orchestrated: add new col → dual write → switch → drop old

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No moment where any running version breaks.

example.outcome: releases where every intermediate state works.

check.q: Why can't distributed systems be upgraded atomically?
check.a: Components deploy independently, so old and new versions inevitably run at the same time.

the-database-problem-migrations-in-cicd.core: Code rolls back in seconds, but data has gravity: schema changes on large tables lock, take time, and can't simply be reverted. Migrations must be versioned, tested, safe online and compatible with both app versions.

first_principles.problem: An ALTER TABLE on 500 million rows locks the table for 40 minutes in production, and 'rollback' would lose new data.
truths: Destructive changes can't be undone without data loss.
Old app versions keep running during deploys.
derivation: Roll **forward** with fix migrations rather than down.

analogy.title: Renovating a load-bearing wall
analogy.story: You can't just undo it; you add supports first, then change it carefully.
analogy.breaks: Down migrations exist, but they rarely restore data, so treat them as last resort.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No write lock, so production keeps running.

check.q: Why is rolling back a migration harder than rolling back code?
check.a: Data written or destroyed by the migration can't simply be restored by reverting files.

the-expand-contract-pattern-parallel-cha.core: Make breaking changes in compatible phases. Expand (add the new structure), migrate (dual-write and backfill, then switch reads), contract (remove the old structure) once nothing uses it. Every phase is deployable and reversible.

first_principles.problem: Renaming a column in one step breaks every app instance still using the old name.
truths: Additive changes are safe for old code.
Removal is safe once nothing references the old structure.
derivation: **Expand**: add the new column; the app writes both.
**Contract**: stop writing the old one, then drop it.

analogy.title: Building a new bridge before demolishing the old one
analogy.story: Traffic keeps flowing on the old bridge until the new one is open and proven.
analogy.breaks: It takes several releases, and dual writes must be kept consistent.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No downtime, and you can stop or roll back at any phase.

check.q: When is it safe to drop the old column?
check.a: Once no running code reads or writes it, after the contract phase deploys everywhere.

decoupling-migrations-jobs-vs-initcontai.core: Run migrations once per release as a dedicated Job (a Helm hook or ArgoCD PreSync), not in initContainers, which run on every pod start and race each other.

first_principles.problem: With 20 replicas, initContainer migrations run 20 times concurrently, causing lock contention, partial runs and crash loops.
truths: A migration should run exactly once per release.
derivation: Use a **Job** or hook before the rollout.
**Gate** the app rollout on the Job's success.
Rely on the migration tool's **locking** (Flyway, Liquibase) as a backstop.

analogy.title: One person updates the shared calendar, not everyone
analogy.story: If all 20 staff edit the calendar at once, it ends up a mess.
analogy.breaks: Jobs need cleanup policies and clear failure handling.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One migration runs, and the app rolls out only on success.

code.text:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: migrate-{{ .Release.Revision }}
  annotations:
    helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade,pre-install
    helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers: [{ name: migrate, image: app:1.5, command: ["flyway", "migrate"] }]

check.q: Why are initContainers poor places for migrations?
check.a: They run on every pod start, so replicas race to apply the same migration.
